sysd-found-124.title: The stub resolver: DNS work done elsewhere
sysd-found-124.text: A stub resolver does almost nothing, on purpose. It moves the resolution work into a name server that supports recursive queries and keeps only a list of such servers. A PC that lacks the resources to resolve names gets an easy way to use DNS. The cache for a whole local network or organization can also be centralized. A simple stub resolver on a home router typically makes a recursive query to the DNS server run by the user's ISP. The drawback is that recursive requests take arbitrary time, so the stub struggles to tune retransmissions for lost UDP packets and dead servers.

sysd-found-104.title: The authoritative name server: the source of truth
sysd-found-104.text:
Every domain has at least one server that speaks for it with final authority. An authoritative name server answers DNS queries only from data configured by an original source, such as the domain administrator. It does not answer from a cache of another server's answers. It publishes information about the domain and about the name servers of any domains below it. It is either primary, holding the original copies of all zone records, or secondary, keeping an identical copy through an automatic updating mechanism in the DNS protocol.

A zone's authoritative servers are stored in the parent zone as NS records. RFC 1034 requires every zone to be available on at least two servers, so it survives host or link failure. Authoritative answers carry the Authoritative Answer (AA) bit. A server named as authoritative for a domain it has no data for causes a lame delegation.

It is usually the resolver's last stop. It holds information specific to its domain, such as the A record, and returns NXDOMAIN if it cannot find the domain.

sysd-found-103.title: Delegation: handing a piece of the namespace to someone else
sysd-found-103.text:
To find www.example.org, a resolver needs ns1.example.org. To find ns1.example.org, it needs example.org first. Delegation has to cope with that loop.

Delegation is the mechanism that assigns responsibility for different parts of the DNS namespace to different name servers. Dividing a zone creates a new one. Authority over it goes to a designated name server, and the parent zone stops being authoritative for it. Each public domain under the TLDs is delegated through an NS record in the parent domain.

An NS record gives a name, not an address. So the resolver must issue another request to find the address of the server it was referred to. If the delegated server is a subdomain of the domain it serves, that is the loop above. The delegating server breaks it by supplying the server's IP addresses as glue. A glue record, a name server paired with its IP address, travels in the additional section of the response. For www.example.org, the org TLD name server includes address records for ns1.example.org along with the delegation.

sysd-found-122.title: DNS zones: who is responsible for which names
sysd-found-122.text:
Cut the DNS tree between any two adjacent nodes, and each connected group of names becomes a zone, authoritative for all names in that region. A zone is a distinct part of the name space delegated to a person, organization or company that maintains it. That organization can change its data unilaterally, grow new sections of the tree, delete nodes or delegate subzones, and larger ones can nest delegations to match their substructure.

A zone's data has four parts, all written as resource records. They are authoritative data for its nodes, data for its top node, data describing delegated subzones, and data giving access to those subzones' name servers. The top node carries NS records listing every server for the zone and a single SOA record of management parameters. Because NS records give no addresses, a zone also holds glue records for servers whose names lie below the cut.

A zone's servers need not sit inside its own domain. One name server for the UK domain is in the US, saving transatlantic bandwidth.

sysd-found-123.title: How a secondary server copies a zone
sysd-found-123.text:
A change made at one server must reach every server for a zone. Changes are made at the primary, typically by editing a master file and then signalling the server to load it. The preferred way to spread them is the DNS protocol's zone transfer, not FTP or ad hoc procedures. This is how a secondary name server polls its primary and copies a changed zone, so every authoritative server for a zone serves the same data.

Secondaries check for changes at a selectable interval by comparing the SERIAL field of the zone's SOA record. The serial must advance whenever the zone changes, so the more recent of two copies can be told apart. The check is a simple query to the primary for the SOA record. If the serial equals the secondary's own, nothing changed and the REFRESH wait restarts.

Three SOA parameters set the rhythm of the checks. A secondary waits REFRESH seconds between checks, retries every RETRY seconds if a check cannot complete, and after EXPIRE seconds without one must discard its copy as obsolete. When the serial shows a change, the secondary sends an AXFR request. The answer is a stream of messages carrying every record of the zone, from which the secondary builds its copy. Because accuracy is essential, AXFR requests must use TCP or another reliable protocol. Secondaries may also run these operations against other secondaries, which helps when the primary is down.

sysd-found-120.title: DNS chooses availability over instant consistency
sysd-found-120.text:
DNS would rather give you an old answer than no answer. RFC 1034 treats access to information as more critical than instantaneous updates or consistency guarantees. So updates percolate out through the users of the system rather than reaching every copy at once. When updates are unavailable because of network or host failure, the usual course is to believe old information while continuing efforts to update it.

The owner of the data sets how stale a copy may get. Copies are distributed with timeouts for refreshing. The distributor sets the timeout and the recipient performs the refresh. Very short intervals can be specified, and the owner can prohibit copies. Most data changes very slowly, such as mailbox bindings and host addresses, but the system must also handle subsets that change on the order of seconds or minutes.

Each organization responsible for a set of domains provides redundant name servers. Every zone must be available on at least two servers, so it stays available despite host or link failure.

sysd-found-196.title: The DNSSEC chain of trust
sysd-found-196.text:
A signature is only as good as the key behind it. An answer can be proved correct only if at least one key or DS record is known to be correct from a source other than DNS. These starting points are trust anchors, typically supplied with the operating system. A chain is a series of linked DS and DNSKEY records from a trust anchor to the domain's authoritative server. Without a complete chain, an answer cannot be securely verified.

Each DS record in a parent zone verifies a DNSKEY record below it. To validate www.example.com, a resolver ideally starts with the DS and DNSKEY at the root. It uses the root's DS for com to verify com's DNSKEY, then example.com's DS and DNSKEY, and finally the RRSIG on the answer. DNSSEC was deployed at the root on July 15, 2010.

A DS record in the parent with no RRSIG in the reply signals a problem. The cause may be someone in the middle stripping the DNSSEC data, a broken server along the path, or a configuration error.

sysd-found-198.title: DNSSEC: proving that a name does not exist
sysd-found-198.text: How do you sign the answer that nothing exists? Proving a name is absent means signing the answer to every query for a non-existent name. That is hard, because DNSSEC was designed for offline signing and it is impossible to pre-generate a response to every hostname. NSEC records link each pair of names in a zone, so a query for k.example.com is answered with an NSEC saying nothing exists between a.example.com and z.example.com. That exposes real names and so allows zone enumeration. NSEC3 hashes the names instead, but GPUs and dedicated hardware let its responses be brute-forced cheaply with offline dictionary attacks.

sysd-found-197.title: DNSSEC keys: signing keys, rollovers and expiry
sysd-found-197.text: DNSSEC uses two kinds of keys. Key signing keys (KSK) sign the DNSKEY records that hold the zone signing keys (ZSK), which sign the other records. ZSKs can be switched more easily and can be shorter, which shrinks RRSIG and DNSKEY records. A new KSK needs its DS record transferred to the parent zone. DS records hold a message digest of the KSK, not the full key, which keeps them small for very large zones such as com. RRSIG records carry absolute timestamps that limit replay. So resolver clocks must be roughly in sync, and a zone must be re-signed regularly or validating resolvers will reject its signatures.

sysd-found-205.title: Split-horizon DNS: different answers for different askers
sysd-found-205.text: The same name can lead to different machines depending on who asks. Split-horizon DNS lets a DNS implementation return different sets of information for the same query, usually chosen by the source address of the request. It manages security and privacy by separating DNS information for internal access from access over an unsecure public network such as the Internet. A common case is a server with both a private LAN address and a public one. The same name resolves to either, depending on the client, so local clients reach it directly with lower latency. Done badly, it can clash with DNSSEC, which vouches for the data returned.

sysd-found-113.title: Inside a DNS message
sysd-found-113.text: Every DNS message, query or response, has the same shape: a header followed by question, answer, authority and additional sections. The header holds Identification, Flags and the counts of questions, answers, authority records and additional records, each field 16 bits long. The identification field matches responses to queries. The flags tell whether the message is a query or reply (QR) and whether the answer is authoritative (AA). They also tell whether it was truncated (TC), and whether recursion is desired (RD) or available (RA). The response code RCODE can be NOERROR (0), FORMERR (1), SERVFAIL (2) or NXDOMAIN (3, nonexistent domain).

sysd-found-127.title: DNS standard queries and inverse queries
sysd-found-127.text: Most DNS traffic is one simple question. A standard query names a domain (QNAME), a record type (QTYPE) and a class (QCLASS), and asks a name server for the matching records. Standard queries are the vast majority of DNS queries, in UDP datagrams or over TCP. A server may add helpful records: a query for the mail-exchange records of ISI.EDU also returns the mail exchangers' addresses. Inverse queries map a resource to the domain names having it, but they are mainly for debugging, are not guaranteed complete, and their results should never be cached. IN-ADDR.ARPA, not inverse queries, is the way to map addresses to host names.

sysd-found-125.title: The resolver's recipe in RFC 1034
sysd-found-125.text: RFC 1034 gives the resolver a four-step recipe. Look for the answer in local information and return it if found. Find the best servers to ask. Send them queries until one responds. Then analyze the response. An answer or name error is cached and returned. A better delegation is cached and the server search repeats. A CNAME is cached and the search restarts at the canonical name. A failed server is dropped and the next tried. Authoritative data is preferred to cached data, and the resolver should bound its work so a loop cannot start.

openers.the-domain-name-system: Computers find each other by number, but people use names, and the Domain Name System translates one into the other. It replaced HOSTS.TXT, a single central file that grew slow and unwieldy with ARPANET, and is now a hierarchical, distributed tree of labels. This chapter covers what a domain publishes in its resource records, from addresses and aliases to mail servers, and who hands out the right to use a name. It also follows the queries themselves, sent over UDP and TCP on port 53 or over encrypted transports. Time to live limits how long answers are kept, and anycast lets servers in many locations share one address.

reviews.the-domain-name-system: DNS trades instant consistency for availability and speed. The tree of names is cut into zones, each delegated to authoritative servers that secondaries keep in step by zone transfer. Every answer carries a TTL, and caches keep most lookups from having to start at a root server. The openness that lets this scale, with unsigned and unencrypted answers, is also its weakness, and DNSSEC answers part of it with a chain of trust and managed keys. Round-robin DNS, anycast and split-horizon answers show how the same system is bent to spread load and to serve different clients differently.
